newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Salang pass wreckage illustrates folly of war.
newsitem.headline: Salang pass wreckage illustrates folly of war.

text.p: In one of the world's great monuments to the folly of war, fire-scorched carcasses of destroyed tanks and skeletal remains of ambushed armoured personnel carriers litter the approach to Afghanistan's Salang pass.

Fifty miles north of Kabul the Salang highway links the capital with northern Afghanistan, climbing through steep switchbacks and a Soviet-built system of tunnels to a height of 3,300 metres before snaking down to the vermilion rice paddies of Pol-e-Khomri.

Fought over virtually non-stop for a generation, the strategic pass is a graveyard commemorating one super-power's ambitions, the fickle nature of Afghanistan's shifting military alliances and the seemingly endless suffering of Afghan civilians.

Moscow poured troops, armour and artillery into central Afghanistan through the Salang during the decade-long Soviet occupation of the country, which finally ended with an humiliating withdrawal in 1989.

Lightly-armed, mobile bands of Afghan mujahideen repeatedly ambushed Soviet convoys up and down the length of the highway during the Soviet era, inflicting heavy casualties before melting away into the mountains to strike again.
Russian tank barrels which once belched fire are now laid as makeshift footbridges across churning mountain streams.
Where mud and stone villages lie destroyed along the route the metal cargo containers which supplied the Soviet army of occupation have been converted into roadside shops and even housing.
Legless war veterans hobbling on crutches are stark reminders of the thousands of land mines laid along the verge of the highway.
Stone cairns mark mark minefields along the worst stretches, but travellers are warned not to step off the pavement anywhere unless in the company of a guide.

If the oldest war debris along the Salang is Soviet, the freshest on the northern side of the pass is from factional fighting between Uzbek warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum and government forces loyal to Tajik defense minister Ahmad Shah Masood.

The two were adversaries along the Salang during the occupation when Masood's troops, operating out of the nearby Panshjer valley, launched hit and run attacks against Soviet forces and their Afghan allies including Dostum.
It was only in 1992 as Kabul was about to fall to the mujahideen that Dostum switched sides.

Rivalry between the two charismatic military leaders erupted in serious fighting along the northern end of the Salang highway earlier this year when Masood attempted to advance from the top of the pass against Dostum's troops to Pol-e-Khomri.
Dostum reprelled the attack but freshly destroyed villages, bomb craters and destroyed equipment flank the highway near Markhan where the fighting was most severe.
When insurgent forces of the conservative Islamic Taleban captured Kabul two weeks ago and Masood's government troops withdrew into the Panshjer, Dostum gained the very top of the Salang pass.
Dostum's soldiers, backed by armour and artillery, are now digging in there in impressive strength.

Below the pass to the south Masood's men are battling Taleban for control of the highway between Salang and Kabul. For the moment at least, Dostum is staying out of the fray, content to let Masood do the fighting and dying.

Resorting to his old tactics, Masood recently ambushed Taleban forces advancing north towards the pass by mining the road behind them and attacking the head of the column -- reportedly killing 200 men and capturing another 100.
